title: Williams v. Walker-Thomas Furniture Co.
summary: The court recognized power to refuse an unconscionable bargain and remanded for findings; it did not itself finally decide that the customers’ contracts were unconscionable.
notes: The editors discuss how allocating payments to the earliest purchases would have allowed ownership of many items to clear. They also present later social and economic accounts of the store’s practices and debates over paternalism; those accounts are not facts found by the appellate court in 1965.

sections.Parties: Walker-Thomas sold household goods on installment terms to Williams and Thorne. After defaults, it sought possession of goods from earlier transactions as well as the latest purchases.
sections.Material Facts:
The printed forms described the transactions as leases, with title transferring only when the required payments had been made. A further clause allocated each payment proportionately across all outstanding purchases. A small balance therefore remained on each item until all purchases were paid off. Buying a new item effectively exposed previously acquired goods to repossession for the new debt.

Williams had reduced the balance from prior purchases to about $164 before buying a stereo priced at $514.95. The seller knew that she supported herself and seven children on a $218 monthly government stipend. After default, the seller sought to repossess goods purchased since 1957. Thorne’s later purchase similarly exposed goods dating from 1958. The issue concerned the operation and presentation of the financing arrangement, not merely whether a court approved of the customers’ choice of household items.
sections.Procedural History: The Court of General Sessions entered judgment for the seller, and the local appellate court affirmed, believing it lacked authority to deny enforcement on this ground. The D.C. Circuit recognized a common-law unconscionability defense and remanded because the lower courts had made no necessary findings. Judge Danaher dissented.
sections.Issue: Could the courts refuse enforcement of an unconscionable agreement under the law applicable when these contracts were made, and what inquiry should govern that determination?
sections.Holding: Yes. Unconscionability present at formation could justify refusing enforcement. The record required further findings before that rule could be applied conclusively.
sections.Reasoning:
The court used the subsequently enacted UCC § 2-302 as persuasive evidence of a principle it could recognize in developing the common law; it did not retroactively apply the statute to these earlier transactions. The relevant inquiry combined lack of meaningful choice with terms unreasonably favorable to the other party. Education, bargaining power, the opportunity to understand the form, hidden terms, and sales practices were relevant to meaningful choice.

Substantive unfairness had to be assessed against the circumstances at formation and the commercial needs and practices of the setting. The decision did not make inability to pay or failure to read an automatic defense. It required an examination of how the obscure payment-allocation and repossession terms operated in these transactions. Because the lower courts believed they could not undertake that inquiry at all, the appellate court could not substitute a final factual determination for them.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Williams joins formation concerns about meaningful assent to a direct review of oppressive terms. Its remand is crucial: recognition of the doctrine and proof that a particular agreement satisfies it are separate steps.

topics.unconscionability: The court identifies both meaningful choice and unreasonably favorable terms as parts of the inquiry.
topics.assent: The manner of presenting and explaining the installment form bears on whether the customer meaningfully accepted its terms.
topics.adhesion: The printed payment-allocation clause creates consequences difficult to see from an individual purchase.
topics.consumer-protection: The opinions debate judicial protection, legislative competence, and the availability of consumer credit.
topics.governing-law: The court uses a later Code provision as persuasive support for common-law development.

learning.separateOpinions: Judge Danaher favored legislative action and a cautious approach. He questioned assumptions about what counted as a luxury, stressed that customers may need installment credit, and worried about consequences for credit availability and many existing transactions.

mnemonic.rationale: A stereo, and everything bought before it
